title: Wi-Fi Fundamentals (802.11)
summary: How Wi-Fi shares the airwaves as a contended medium, and the practical model behind "why is my Wi-Fi slow."

slides.markdown:
**Wi-Fi** (the 802.11 family of standards) is wireless Ethernet sharing one radio medium among every nearby device — unlike wired Ethernet where each cable is a private link, every device on a Wi-Fi network is quite literally talking over the same air.

- Devices take turns using the shared airwaves — they can't all transmit at once without colliding.
- "More bars" measures signal *strength*, not the bandwidth actually available to you.
- WPA2/WPA3 handle encryption and access control over that shared medium.

Wired Ethernet gives each device (mostly) its own physical link to a switch — collisions are largely a non-issue on modern switched networks. Wi-Fi can't do that: every device within range of an access point shares the **same radio-frequency medium**. Only one device can transmit on a given channel at a time without garbling both transmissions.

This explains almost everything distinctive about Wi-Fi: why more devices on one AP means less airtime per device, and why a busy coffee shop's Wi-Fi degrades even with a fast internet connection behind it.

Wired Ethernet used CSMA/**CD** — Collision *Detection*: transmit, and if a collision happens, detect it and retransmit. Wi-Fi can't detect a collision while transmitting — a radio can't hear another device's signal while its own is on the air.

So Wi-Fi uses CSMA/**CA** — Collision *Avoidance*: listen first, wait for the channel to be idle, then wait a small random backoff before transmitting. It's more conservative than wired Ethernet, part of why real Wi-Fi throughput sits below advertised speed. See [ethernet-mac-addressing](ethernet-mac-addressing).

slides.subTitle: SSID vs BSSID
slides.markdown:
![A device associating with an access point: SSID broadcast, authentication, then association](assets/wifi-ap-association.svg)

The **SSID** is the human-readable network name ("CoffeeShop-Guest"); the **BSSID** is the AP's actual MAC address identifying that specific radio. A device picks a network by SSID, but **associates** with one specific BSSID — which matters when one SSID is broadcast by several APs (a mesh network or enterprise deployment) and the device has to choose the best one.

assets.alt: A device associating with an access point: SSID broadcast, authentication, then association

slides.markdown:
| | 2.4GHz | 5GHz | 6GHz |
|---|---|---|
| Range | Longest (penetrates walls better) | Shorter | Shortest |
| Speed | Lowest | Higher | Highest |
| Interference | Heavy — Bluetooth, microwaves, older devices | Less crowded | Least crowded (newest, fewer devices support it) |

**How to decide:** 2.4GHz for range through walls and older/IoT devices; 5GHz as the everyday sweet spot for laptops/phones; 6GHz (Wi-Fi 6E/7 only) when you need maximum throughput at short range with minimal interference from neighbors.

Each band is divided into **channels** — narrower frequency slices an AP can operate on. In 2.4GHz, channels are so close together that only **1, 6, and 11** don't overlap with each other in the US; picking, say, channel 4 means overlapping with both neighbors' traffic, adding interference even if you're on a "different" channel.

5GHz has far more non-overlapping channels, one reason it performs better in dense environments like apartment buildings — not just because of less interference from other devices, but because there's simply more usable spectrum to spread across.

Wi-Fi signal strength falls off with more than raw distance:

- **Distance** — signal strength drops roughly with the square of distance.
- **Walls/materials** — concrete and metal attenuate far more than drywall; a router two rooms away through concrete can be worse than one twice as far with clear line of sight.
- **Interference** — other Wi-Fi networks, Bluetooth, even microwaves (2.4GHz) competing for the same spectrum, degrading throughput even when signal *strength* looks fine.

This is why signal bars alone are a poor proxy for actual usable bandwidth.

- **WPA2** (2004) — still widely deployed, uses AES, but its 4-way handshake is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks against weak passwords (KRACK exploited a separate flaw in its handshake logic).
- **WPA3** (2018) — replaces the handshake with **SAE**, which resists offline password-guessing even against a captured handshake, and mandates stronger encryption for enterprise deployments.

WPA3 closes real, previously-exploited weaknesses in WPA2 — prefer it wherever devices support it.

![Several devices on one access point taking turns via CSMA/CA airtime contention](assets/wifi-airtime-contention.svg)

Every additional active device on an AP means more contention for the same shared airtime — a single device streaming 4K video can noticeably slow down everyone else on that AP, even though nothing about their *own* connection changed.

assets.alt: Several devices on one access point taking turns via CSMA/CA airtime contention

slides.subTitle: Bars aren't bandwidth
slides.markdown: A very common misconception: **"full signal bars means I should be getting full speed."** Signal bars measure **signal strength** (how clearly your device can hear the AP) — they say nothing about how many other devices are contending for that AP's airtime, how congested the channel is from neighboring networks, or how much actual bandwidth the AP's backhaul (its own connection to the internet) has. A device can show 5 bars sitting right next to a congested, overloaded AP and still get poor throughput — strength and available bandwidth are genuinely different things.
